question: Can one accelerate optimization beyond Fisher natural gradient by factoring an objective as L(x)=Lbar(f(x)), choosing a convenient metric in a simpler reference space, pulling that metric back through f, and solving the resulting preconditioned direction?

key_findings.claim: The central construction is a pullback preconditioner, and its Hessian choice is the generalized Gauss-Newton form rather than a new generalization unique to natural gradient.
key_findings.evidence: Writing J=df/dx, Equation 9 defines Gx=J^T Gy J. With Euclidean Gy this is the ordinary Gram/Gauss-Newton matrix J^T J; with Gy equal to the Hessian of Lbar it is J^T Hess(Lbar) J, the generalized Gauss-Newton curvature for the composite objective. The paper cites broad natural-gradient background but does not identify this exact relationship or compare against prior pullback-metric and general-similarity natural-gradient frameworks.

key_findings.claim: Positive definiteness in the reference space does not make the pulled-back object a Riemannian metric, and two of the three experiments make it singular by construction.
key_findings.evidence: For positive-definite Gy, J^T Gy J is positive definite only when J has full column rank. The paper instead asks f to be relatively surjective, which does not remove a parameter-space kernel. In the spin experiment f(Si)=Si/||Si|| annihilates every radial direction; in the eigenvalue experiment f(x)=x/||x|| annihilates x itself. Normalized MPS states also have scale and tensor-gauge redundancies. Thus Gx is positive semidefinite and Equation 14 has non-unique parameter solutions unless a pseudoinverse, quotient/gauge treatment, or parameter-space damping is specified; none is.

key_findings.claim: The appendix proves only a local projected-direction identity, not the claimed faster convergence or escape from local minima.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A argues that the push-forward of a pullback-natural-gradient direction is the Gy-orthogonal projection of the reference-space direction onto im(df), under a full-rank restricted-system assumption. It supplies no descent theorem, convergence rate, iteration complexity, line-search conditions, basin analysis, or stochastic result. The main-text criteria use undefined relations such as 'relatively surjective', 'close', and direction similarity to a known global minimizer. Raw arrows to xmin are also not a generally defined tangent direction on an arbitrary Riemannian manifold. Consequently the sentence that the method is proved to converge faster and the suggestion that it escapes local minima exceed the proof.

anchors.section: Global direction criterion and claimed proof

key_findings.claim: The written algorithm is internally inconsistent about the descent direction and cannot be implemented exactly from the paper.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 5-6 apply max rather than argmax while treating its result as a vector. Equation 7 gives the expected negative direction -G^-1 grad L, but the algorithm text and Equation 14 solve G dx=+grad L with no minus sign before line search. Appendix A repeats the max-versus-argmax notation and alternates signed and unsigned reference directions. These may be typographical errors, but in the absence of code or pseudocode they leave the executable update ambiguous.

key_findings.claim: The least-squares example is one unreplicated synthetic trace and does not validate quantum-state purification.
key_findings.evidence: The experiment takes a length-40 Heisenberg-chain ground state, adds independent numbers in (-0.1,0.1) to every element of its two-site reduced density matrices, and fits an MPS of bond dimension 5. Arbitrary elementwise noise need not preserve Hermiticity, positivity, unit trace, or cross-marginal consistency, so the inputs are not shown to be physical mixed-state marginals. Figure 5 reports cost versus outer iteration for one unspecified draw and initialization, without state fidelity, observable error, constraint residual, seed variation, or a real device-noise model.

key_findings.claim: The minimum-eigenvalue experiment does not define a valid Fisher-information baseline and uses target information to construct its proposed metric.
key_findings.evidence: The paper calls rho_i=x_i/Z a probability with Z=sqrt(sum_i x_i^2), although an arbitrary real x has negative components and sum_i x_i/Z is generally not one; log rho_i in the Fisher definition can therefore be undefined. If squared amplitudes were intended, both the distribution and Fisher calculation would change. The proposed metric is H+epsilon I pulled back through x/||x||, while epsilon is chosen from the most negative Hessian eigenvalue even though the benchmark's objective is to find the minimum eigenvalue. The statement that a rough value can first be obtained by gradient descent excludes that preliminary solve from the plotted comparison. The distribution, symmetry, seed, and initialization of the 1000-by-1000 random matrix are also absent.

anchors.section: Minimal eigen-value of a given matrix

key_findings.claim: The plotted iteration advantage is not a computational-efficiency comparison because every proposed outer step contains an uncounted linear solve.
key_findings.evidence: The method forms matrix-vector products and invokes conjugate gradient to solve the pullback system before an outer line search, but Figures 5-7 count only outer optimization steps. The paper reports no inner-CG iterations or tolerance, metric-vector cost, Hessian-eigenvalue estimation, tensor-contraction cost, wall time, memory, hardware, or function/gradient evaluation counts. A proposed step can therefore cost many baseline steps, especially for Hilbert-space and density-matrix maps, so fewer plotted steps do not establish faster computation.

key_findings.claim: The three demonstrations show curve-level feasibility on hand-designed problems, not universality across optimization tasks.
key_findings.evidence: Each reference map is chosen using privileged structure: reduced marginals or amplitudes for the MPS problem, exact spin normalization for the classical model, and exact vector normalization plus the target matrix for the Rayleigh quotient. There is one instance per setting, no blind metric-selection rule, no held-out task family, no adversarial or ill-conditioned case, and no comparison with Newton, generalized Gauss-Newton, L-BFGS, trust-region, mirror-descent, or modern natural-gradient approximations. The evidence supports that tailored preconditioners can reduce outer iterations, which is much narrower than a systematic universal method.

key_findings.claim: Figure 6 visually supports a large error reduction on one classical-spin instance, but its experimental protocol and statistical reliability are unreported.
key_findings.evidence: On the log-scale plot through 60 outer steps, the green proposed curve ends below 10^-4, while nonlinear CG is around 10^-2 and gradient descent remains higher. The paper gives a 50-by-50 lattice but omits boundary conditions, initial spin distribution, random seed, exact line-search rule, stopping tolerance, damping value, repetitions, dispersion, and cost per step. The caption also cross-references the later Rayleigh-quotient equation rather than the spin energy. Exact curve values are not tabulated.

key_findings.claim: The canonical artifact is not sufficient to reproduce any of the three numerical results.
key_findings.evidence: The official arXiv v1 source contains the TeX manuscript, bibliography, and static figure files only. It links no repository, dataset, environment, implementation, numerical table, or plotting script, and an exact-title GitHub repository search returned no result on the audit date. Missing details include initializations, seeds, matrix generator, MPS ground-state generator, boundary conditions, line-search schedule, inner-CG tolerance and budget, stopping rules, damping values by experiment, trial count, hardware, and raw curves. No uncertainty is shown anywhere.

method.core_idea: Represent a composite objective through a simpler reference manifold, choose a geometry in that reference space, and pull it back through the model map so parameter updates follow a locally steep reference-space direction rather than Euclidean parameter gradient.
method.mechanism: For L(x)=Lbar(f(x)), let J be the Jacobian of f and choose Gy as either the identity or Hess(Lbar)+epsilon I. Form Gx=J^T Gy J, solve a linear system for a metric-preconditioned parameter direction with conjugate gradient, normalize the direction, and conduct a line search. Its push-forward J dx is intended to equal the Gy-orthogonal projection of the reference natural-gradient direction onto the attainable tangent image. Examples instantiate f as two-site density matrices, normalized or unnormalized MPS amplitudes, normalized classical spins, and a normalized Rayleigh-quotient vector.
assumptions: The objective factors differentiably as Lbar composed with a reference map f whose geometry is simpler than the parameter-space objective.
A useful reference-space metric can be selected manually from identity or a shifted Hessian.
The reference map is sufficiently expressive near a desired solution and maps the parameter optimum near a reference-space optimum.
The Jacobian image captures the desired reference descent direction well enough that projection does not remove essential progress.
The pulled-back matrix is invertible or an unspecified linear solver convention resolves its null space.
A minimum Hessian eigenvalue can be estimated accurately enough to make the shifted Hessian positive definite.
Normalized directions and an unspecified line search make outer iteration counts comparable across metrics.
Single synthetic problem instances reflect broader optimization behavior.

techniques.role: Factor the objective through a physically meaningful output or ansatz space.
Construct parameter curvature as J^T Gy J from the chosen reference geometry.
Recover a Gram or Gauss-Newton preconditioner from Euclidean reference geometry.
Use shifted reference-loss curvature to form a generalized Gauss-Newton preconditioner.
Compute an outer search direction through matrix-free conjugate-gradient solves.
Normalize each direction and select an outer update length.
Parameterize a length-40 quantum state with bond dimension 5 in the least-squares example.
Map unconstrained three-vectors to unit classical spins before optimizing antiferromagnetic energy.
Map a vector to the unit sphere for minimum-Rayleigh-quotient optimization.
Inspect all eight rendered pages, Figures 1-8, Table I, axes, legends, captions, and equation cross-references.
Inspect the official arXiv source bundle and search for an official implementation or numerical artifacts.

evaluations.setting: Length-40 one-dimensional antiferromagnetic Heisenberg ground-state marginals perturbed elementwise by uniform noise in (-0.1,0.1), reconstructed with an MPS of bond dimension 5.
evaluations.metric: Least-squares cost versus outer optimization step.
evaluations.result: Figure 5 shows four pullback-metric variants descending faster and ending below the displayed gradient-descent and nonlinear-CG traces; exact values, physical reconstruction metrics, compute cost, and uncertainty are absent.
evaluations.baseline: Euclidean gradient descent and nonlinear conjugate gradient on the same unspecified realization.

evaluations.setting: A 50-by-50 two-dimensional classical Heisenberg antiferromagnet represented by unconstrained vectors normalized inside the energy.
evaluations.metric: Absolute relative energy error against the stated exact antiferromagnetic minimum versus outer step.
evaluations.result: By step 60, the proposed curve is visually below 10^-4 while CG is around 10^-2 and gradient descent is higher; there is one curve per method, no raw table, and no runtime or repeated-trial result.
evaluations.baseline: Gradient descent and nonlinear conjugate gradient.

evaluations.setting: Minimum Rayleigh quotient of one unspecified 1000-by-1000 real random matrix described only as not positive definite.
evaluations.metric: Absolute relative objective error against the exact minimum eigenvalue versus outer step.
evaluations.result: The proposed green curve falls almost vertically to approximately 10^-12 at the plot's left edge; the paper says CG reaches 10^-12 after about 125 steps while gradient descent remains much worse at 300. Inner-solve work and preliminary minimum-eigenvalue estimation are not counted.
evaluations.baseline: Gradient descent, an asserted Fisher-natural-gradient equivalent, and nonlinear conjugate gradient.

limitations: Author-stated: selecting the reference manifold requires experience and problem understanding.
Reviewer-identified: the central criteria of good, relatively surjective, close, and direction similarity are not quantitatively defined.
Reviewer-identified: no convergence, rate, complexity, or local-minimum-escape theorem is supplied.
Reviewer-identified: positive-definite reference metrics pull back to singular matrices in the normalized-spin, normalized-vector, and gauge-redundant MPS examples.
Reviewer-identified: no pseudoinverse, quotient geometry, gauge fixing, or parameter-space damping resolves those null directions.
Reviewer-identified: the executable update has sign and max-versus-argmax inconsistencies across Equations 5-7, 14, and Appendix A.
Reviewer-identified: the eigenvalue example's rho_i=x_i/||x|| is not a valid probability distribution for arbitrary real x, so its Fisher baseline is undefined as written.
Reviewer-identified: choosing the eigenvalue-example shift from the most negative Hessian eigenvalue uses information closely tied to the target solution.
Reviewer-identified: arbitrary elementwise density-matrix noise is not shown to preserve quantum-state validity.
Reviewer-identified: only one problem instance and one trajectory per setting are displayed, without seeds, repetitions, uncertainty, or robustness sweeps.
Reviewer-identified: outer steps ignore inner linear-solve and metric-construction costs; wall time, memory, and evaluation counts are missing.
Reviewer-identified: the baselines omit generalized Gauss-Newton, Newton/truncated Newton, L-BFGS, trust-region, mirror-descent, and scalable natural-gradient methods.
Reviewer-identified: the official artifact provides no code, raw data, environment, or complete experiment recipe.
failure_modes: A non-injective reference map produces a singular pullback, causing standard conjugate gradient or an explicit inverse to be undefined or initialization-dependent in the null space.
A nearly rank-deficient Jacobian makes the inner system ill-conditioned and can erase any outer-iteration advantage through many matrix-vector products.
Projection onto im(df) can discard most of an otherwise favorable reference direction when the ansatz tangent space is poorly aligned.
An indefinite or inaccurately shifted reference Hessian makes the matrix unsuitable for ordinary CG and can produce ascent or unstable directions.
The sign omission in Equation 14 can turn the intended descent step into ascent if implemented literally.
A manually chosen reference map can encode privileged knowledge of the answer and look effective on a handcrafted instance without transferring to a new task.
Elementwise perturbation can yield nonphysical density matrices, letting low optimization cost masquerade as successful purification.
Invalid probabilities or negative components make the asserted Fisher information undefined in the eigenvalue comparison.
Estimating the smallest Hessian eigenvalue for damping can cost as much as the target optimization or fail to guarantee positive definiteness when underestimated.
Normalized outer-step plots can reverse method rankings when inner solves, line-search evaluations, and metric construction are counted.
Multiple global minima, quotient symmetries, or a manifold cut locus make a raw direction 'toward xmin' ambiguous or non-unique.
A tailored metric can converge rapidly to a poor local minimum because the projection identity alone gives no global basin guarantee.
reusable_insights: Treat reference-space geometry as a generalized Gauss-Newton design problem: specify the output map, metric, damping, and solver independently behind modular interfaces.
Check Jacobian rank and known invariances before calling J^T Gy J a metric; use quotient coordinates, gauge fixing, pseudoinverses, or explicit parameter damping where needed.
Define the projected direction with an explicit weighted least-squares problem, which makes signs, pseudoinverse conventions, and null-space behavior testable.
Benchmark curvature methods by wall time, matrix-vector products, gradient/function evaluations, memory, and inner residual, not just outer iterations.
Separate the cost of estimating damping or spectral bounds from the optimization run and compare fixed, adaptive, and trust-region regularization fairly.
Validate metric-selection rules on preregistered task families with held-out maps and conditioning regimes, rather than only hand-designed examples.
For quantum reconstruction, generate valid channels or mixed states and report positivity, trace, Hermiticity, marginal consistency, state fidelity, and observable errors.
Use symmetric, seeded matrix ensembles and publish spectra, initial vectors, raw trajectories, and exact stopping rules for eigenvalue benchmarks.
Compare identity and Hessian pullbacks directly with Gauss-Newton, generalized Gauss-Newton, truncated Newton, L-BFGS, and trust-region baselines.
Report convergence across seeds and problem instances with confidence intervals because preconditioner success can depend strongly on initialization and spectrum.
Release a minimal matrix-free operator API, immutable configs, tests for sign/descent and null spaces, and scripts that regenerate every curve.
open_questions: Under what verifiable rank, smoothness, and alignment conditions does a reference pullback yield global or local convergence improvements?
Can a quotient-manifold or minimum-norm formulation make the MPS, spin, and Rayleigh examples mathematically well defined under their exact symmetries?
How should one learn or select a reference metric without using the unknown optimizer or its smallest Hessian eigenvalue?
Does the method still win when inner-CG work, line searches, spectral estimates, contractions, and memory are included?
How sensitive are results to damping, solver tolerance, initialization, Jacobian rank, condition number, and reference-map perturbations?
Can an adaptive metric remain positive definite and coordinate invariant for nonconvex reference losses?
Would a standard generalized Gauss-Newton or trust-region implementation reproduce all three reported curves?
Do valid quantum noise channels and physically constrained marginals preserve the apparent advantage in the MPS task?
Can reference maps be discovered on held-out optimization families and then transferred without expert redesign?
What failure detector should fall back to a first-order method when the projected reference direction is poorly aligned or the pullback solve stagnates?
Can scalable Woodbury, Nyström, or structured approximations preserve the direction while providing auditable error-cost tradeoffs?

competitive_landscape.title: New insights and perspectives on the natural gradient method
competitive_landscape.difference: Martens shows when Fisher natural gradient equals generalized Gauss-Newton, analyzes parameterization invariance and convergence, and motivates damping and trust regions. Dong et al.'s Hessian pullback is the same J^T H J composite curvature pattern, but their paper neither identifies that equivalence nor supplies the regularization and theory needed for a robust optimizer.

competitive_landscape.title: A Formalization of The Natural Gradient Method for General Similarity Measures
competitive_landscape.difference: Mallasto, Dela Haije, and Feragen derive natural-gradient metrics from arbitrary similarity measures and explicitly connect them to existing optimization techniques. That predates the reviewed claim that metrics beyond Fisher can be chosen systematically; Dong et al. instead start from a manually selected reference manifold and provide quantum-inspired examples, but omit this closest conceptual prior.

competitive_landscape.title: Optimal transport natural gradient for statistical manifolds with continuous sample space
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen and Li pull the Wasserstein metric from distribution space to parameters, state positive-definiteness conditions, derive the gradient flow, prove asymptotic Newton-like behavior for a Wasserstein objective, and test multiple statistical families. Dong et al. generalize the choice of reference space informally, but their maps are often non-injective and their pullbacks therefore fail to be Riemannian metrics without additional treatment.

competitive_landscape.title: Riemannian Natural Gradient Methods
competitive_landscape.difference: Hu et al. formulate natural gradient when the parameter domain itself is Riemannian, prove almost-sure global convergence and local linear or quadratic rates under explicit assumptions, and evaluate large-scale learning problems. The reviewed paper uses manifold language but raw coordinate updates, undefined global arrows, and no retraction or convergence theorem.

competitive_landscape.title: Achieving High Accuracy with PINNs via Energy Natural Gradients
competitive_landscape.difference: Müller and Zeinhofer use an energy Hessian as a function-space Riemannian metric, prove that the pushed-forward direction is a projected Newton direction, and benchmark PINNs and Deep Ritz against standard optimizers with released code. It turns Dong et al.'s informal Hessian-pullback intuition into a precise task-specific algorithm with quantitative accuracy evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Improving Energy Natural Gradient Descent through Woodbury, Momentum, and Randomization
competitive_landscape.difference: Guzmán-Cordero et al. attack the uncounted inner-solve cost directly with Woodbury reformulation, momentum, subsampling, and randomized solvers, reporting matched L2 error up to 75 times faster than original ENGD. The reviewed work counts only outer steps and therefore cannot establish the corresponding accuracy-cost advantage.

competitive_landscape.title: Natural gradient descent with momentum
competitive_landscape.difference: Nouy and Somacal formulate natural gradient for differentiably parameterized nonlinear function manifolds, including tensor networks, and add Heavy-Ball/Nesterov-style inertia while explicitly noting that projected natural gradients can still enter local minima or be nonoptimal. This directly tempers Dong et al.'s local-minimum rhetoric and extends the same function-space projection view algorithmically.

competitive_landscape.title: Energy Manifold Natural Gradient Descent: Riemannian Optimization for Neural PDE Solvers
competitive_landscape.difference: Liang and Gao restrict an energy-induced quadratic model to feasible tangent directions, use retractions, prove coordinate invariance and global first-order convergence, handle inexact solves, and derive exact Woodbury plus controlled Nyström approximations. It supplies the manifold correctness, solver diagnostics, and convergence guarantees absent from Dong et al.'s heuristic pullback recipe.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A unified method extends natural gradient beyond Fisher information by selecting a suitable reference Riemannian manifold, pulling its metric back to parameters, and obtaining faster convergence on least-squares, classical-spin, and eigenvalue problems.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper writes the pullback formula, derives a projected reference-direction identity, instantiates identity and shifted-Hessian metrics, and shows three sets of single-run outer-iteration curves where tailored metrics descend faster than gradient descent and nonlinear conjugate gradient.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The most useful contribution is a compact quantum-physics-oriented illustration of choosing geometry in an ansatz output space. The mathematical novelty is limited: pullback metrics predate the paper, identity pullbacks are Gauss-Newton, Hessian pullbacks are generalized Gauss-Newton, and a prior work already formalized natural gradients for general similarity measures. Moreover, the presented pullbacks are singular in the normalized examples, the Fisher comparator is invalid as written, and no convergence or cost-normalized evidence substantiates the broad universality claim. The result is best treated as a heuristic design note rather than a validated general optimizer.

reviewer_notes: Primary audit covered all eight pages of arXiv v1, every panel and caption of Figures 1-8, Table I, equations, appendix, and references. Figures 5-7 were inspected at original rendered resolution; approximate plotted orders are reported only where visually unambiguous, and no curve was digitized. The official source archive was inspected: it contains NG.tex, bibliographies, one PNG, and four figure PDFs, but no code, data, configuration, numeric results, supplement, or repository URL. An exact-title GitHub repository search returned zero repositories on 2026-08-23, so the record says no official linked implementation rather than claiming that no private or differently named code exists. Competitor research used primary arXiv/PMLR records and exact current versions through 2026-08-23, spanning generalized Gauss-Newton equivalence, general-similarity and Wasserstein pullbacks, rigorous Riemannian natural gradient, Hessian-induced energy metrics, scalable solvers, momentum, tensor networks, and current manifold formulations.
